description: Etsuko, Hanako, Reiko and the North Korean officials and detainees they encounter.
content_html:
A Family Divided by a Coastline

Francis Turnly’s characters in The Great Wave carry the weight of a documented historical event. They are not simply dramatic constructs — they are theatrical representations of a human situation that was real for many families along Japan’s western coast in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Understanding how to perform and design these characters requires understanding both their individual psychology and their structural function in the parallel storylines. Every character exists on at least two levels: as a human being with specific desires and fears, and as an embodiment of a political relationship between two states.

Hanako: The Anchoring Figure

Hanako is 17 when she is abducted. She is the play’s central figure but also, by design, its most constrained: the physical fact of captivity means she rarely initiates action. Her dramatic arc is internal — the slow, painful accommodation to a life she did not choose, and the question of whether accommodation equals surrender or survival. A performer playing Hanako across the play’s full timeline faces one of the most demanding tasks in the GCSE set-play canon: communicating 24 years of interior change through vocal interpretation and physical evolution, without the luxury of a narrator explaining the psychological shifts.

In the early captivity scenes, a performer might play Hanako with a fast, shallow breath pattern — higher pitch, clipped phrasing, physical restlessness. She paces: she is young, frightened, disoriented. A decade later, the same performer must communicate containment without defeat. A slower pace of speech, longer pauses before responding to her captors, a more upright but very still posture — the body has learned economy, not submission. The key performance challenge is distinguishing accommodation from defeat; Hanako survives precisely because she internalises rather than breaks.

Key Fact

Hanako is the play’s emotional centre across two decades. A performer must track her ageing through specific vocal and physical changes rather than relying on costume or make-up alone: pace of speech, range of movement, and the quality of stillness are the primary tools.

Reiko: The Advocate

Reiko is Hanako’s older sister, and the last person to see Hanako before the abduction. Her arc is the inverse of Hanako’s: where Hanako is confined and controlled, Reiko becomes increasingly active, increasingly public. She refuses the easy conclusion — that Hanako drowned — and her refusal drives the Japanese storyline. A performer playing Reiko must chart a different kind of psychological journey: from grief-stricken teenager to determined adult campaigner, without losing the underlying guilt of their last argument.

In the early scenes, Reiko’s physicality might be collapsed, withdrawn, directed downward — the proxemics of grief. A performer might keep her consistently downstage right, nearer the audience but turned slightly away from the other family members — present but unreachable. In the later scenes, her energy redirects into forward motion and direct eye contact: she stands upstage centre and addresses other characters (or, in moments of direct appeal, the audience itself) with a sustained, level gaze. The posture opens, the volume increases, the pacing quickens when bureaucratic silence is confronted.

Etsuko: The Mother

Etsuko, the mother, undergoes the most visible ageing across the play. She begins as an anxious parent in middle age and ends as an elderly woman whose grief has become the shape of her life. For a costume designer, Etsuko presents an opportunity to communicate temporal change through fabric and silhouette: a domestic, practical mid-layer in the early scenes — apron, layered cottons, a dark headscarf — might give way, scene by scene, to heavier, darker fabrics that seem to weigh the body down. Hair and make-up contribute here: progressively lighter powder, more drawn lines around the eyes, slower application of movement.

For a lighting designer, Etsuko’s scenes in Japan offer the opportunity to use a warm but increasingly low-intensity lighting wash to suggest domestic space becoming emotionally colder over time. The colour temperature of the Japan sequences might shift imperceptibly from amber to a neutral white over the course of the play — so subtle that the audience feels the change before they can name it.

A common performance error for Etsuko is to play her as uniformly sad from the start. This flattens the arc. In the early scenes, Etsuko may be partly in denial — performing domestic normality — which means a performer might actually increase the pace and volume of her housekeeping activities, her insistence on routine, as a defence against grief. The breaks in this routine — the moments she stops mid-task and simply stands still — carry the greater emotional weight precisely because the activity around them has been lively. A Stanislavskian approach to Etsuko means identifying her given circumstances precisely for each scene: where is she in the emotional timeline? What does she still believe at this point? What has she been told? Has she yet seen the government’s documentation? Each answer changes what the body and voice do.

Kum-Chol and the Question of the Captor

Kum-Chol is the North Korean officer who oversees Hanako’s captivity. He is one of the most demanding characters in the play to perform because Turnly resists making him simply a villain. He is complicit in a state crime, but he is also recognisably human: he has loyalties, beliefs and, perhaps, moments of doubt. A performer playing Kum-Chol must avoid the trap of playing ideological certainty as blankness. The most interesting choices for this character involve gestus — the specific way his body communicates his relationship to institutional authority. He stands a particular way when reading official orders; he moves differently when alone with Hanako. These physical contrasts are where performance becomes analysis.

Jung Sun and the Teaching Scenes

Jung Sun is a North Korean assigned to learn Japanese from Hanako. The relationship that develops between them is the play’s most nuanced portrayal of what coercion does to human bonds. He is not free either — both of them are in the grip of the same state machinery — but his situation is different. For a director, the teaching scenes are among the most choreographically rich in the play: two people sitting across a table, both pretending a neutrality neither feels, in a space that is simultaneously a classroom and a prison. The proxemics here carry enormous weight. A director might begin with the performers at maximum downstage distance from each other and have them gradually, scene by scene, reduce that distance — a physical narrative of reluctant trust.

Key Fact

The play’s character relationships are built on constrained proximity: nearly every significant pairing is between people in unequal power positions. Proxemics — the distance between performers and whether it changes — is the most direct way to communicate these power dynamics in staging.

Examiners note that students frequently describe Hanako as ‘sad’ or ‘broken’ throughout the play and treat this as a sufficient performance analysis. It is not. The specific vocal and physical journey from frightened teenager to quietly resilient adult requires different, concrete choices at different points in the timeline. ‘Sad’ is an emotion; examiners want to know how you would embody it: lowered volume, longer inhalations before speaking, a reduced gestural range, avoidance of direct eye contact with authority figures. And crucially, these choices must change across the timeline — not because Hanako becomes happy, but because her psychological strategy evolves. A student who tracks this evolution scene by scene, with specific choices, is writing at the highest level.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark performer questions on The Great Wave, the most common error is writing ‘I would say it sadly’ or ‘I would look upset’ without naming a specific vocal skill (pace, volume, pitch, pause) or physical skill (posture, gesture, proxemics, eye contact) anchored to a named moment of the play. The question asks you to demonstrate that you understand how performance communicates meaning — not just what the character feels but how the audience sees and hears that feeling. A strong answer for a question about Hanako in the first interrogation scene would specify: reduced volume (near-whisper) to communicate internalised fear; upright but rigid posture with hands kept still to suggest controlled suppression of panic; the performer positioned downstage centre with interrogators in a semi-circle behind — proxemically surrounded, yet facing front to give the audience access to the face. Name the moment, name the choice, name the effect.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hanako’s arc is internal — a 24-year journey from disoriented teenager to quietly resilient adult, communicated through specific, evolving vocal and physical choices rather than uniform sadness.
  • Reiko and Etsuko on the Japanese side mirror Hanako’s journey in contrasting directions: Reiko becomes increasingly outward and active; Etsuko becomes increasingly weighted and still.
  • Kum-Chol and Jung Sun are not simply antagonists — their complexity requires gestus-led performance choices that distinguish institutional role from individual humanity.

practice_questions.text: Name Hanako's older sister in The Great Wave.
What is meant by the term 'proxemics' in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying proxemics as the physical distance between performers; 1 mark for explaining that it communicates relationship, power or emotion between characters.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer could use fabric and silhouette to communicate Etsuko's ageing across the play. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific costume approach for Etsuko (1); naming of a fabric, colour or silhouette choice for an early scene (1); description of how this changes in a later scene (1); explanation of what effect the visual progression creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly uses the character of Kum-Chol to present a morally complex view of complicity and institutional authority.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that Kum-Chol is complicit in a state crime but is not portrayed as simply villainous (1); analysis of the performative implication of this complexity, e.g. gestus choices that distinguish official role from individual moments (1); reference to a specific staging moment or scene (1); explanation of the effect this ambiguity creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Hanako in the first interrogation scene, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate the tension between outward submission and inward resistance. Refer to at least one specific vocal skill and one physical skill.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both a concrete vocal skill (e.g. near-whispered volume with controlled, level intonation to imply disciplined suppression rather than passive fear; deliberate pauses before answering to suggest internal negotiation) and a concrete physical skill (e.g. upright but entirely still posture, hands flat on the table, maintaining eye contact with interrogators only when directly addressed) are named and justified with reference to this scene. The effect on the audience is specified: watching a young woman calculate her survival in real time. Secure: One concrete vocal and one physical choice with generally accurate effect; may be less specific about the moment. Developing: Describes what the character feels but translates this into generic choices (speaks quietly, looks scared) with no named moment. Emerging: Identifies the emotional state with no performance translation.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the teaching scenes between Hanako and Jung Sun to communicate the gradual shift in their relationship from coerced formality to reluctant human connection. Consider the use of proxemics, levels, blocking and at least one design element. Refer to specific moments within the scenes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A sustained, specific discussion of the teaching scenes as a choreographic arc. Proxemics choices are concrete and tracked across multiple scenes (starting distance named in metres or spatial terms, reducing across scenes). Levels are used deliberately (e.g. both seated at a table establishes equality of constraint; one standing mid-scene shifts power briefly). Blocking describes specific moves (e.g. Hanako begins each lesson by sitting on the far edge of the desk, Jung Sun facing her from across; by a later scene, she has shifted to the same side of the table to correct his pronunciation). At least one design element is specific: lighting (e.g. a neutral 4200K overhead state for the formal lessons, softening to a warmer, lower-intensity Fresnel as the relationship develops); or sound (the ambient propaganda music audible in earlier lessons gradually dropping in volume as the scenes progress, suggesting the gradual reduction of the state’s presence in the space between them). Effect on audience is specified at each stage. Substantiated judgement about what the staging is arguing about coercion and human connection. Secure: Two or three staging choices across the scenes, mostly concrete, at least one design element, generally accurate effect. Developing: Aware of the proxemic opportunity but describes changes in general terms; limited design detail. Emerging: Describes the scene as a classroom with limited staging analysis.

knowledge_checks.q: What is Hanako's role at the start of The Great Wave?
options: A 17-year-old Japanese student abducted by North Korean agents
A Japanese diplomat negotiating for abductees
A teacher in a Japanese school

knowledge_checks.q: What is gestus in Brechtian performance?
options: A lighting technique using a gobo to project texture
A Stanislavskian technique for emotional memory
A physical posture or gesture expressing a character's social attitude
A sound design term for a recurring musical motif

knowledge_checks.q: Proxemics refers to the physical _____ between performers on stage, which communicates power and relationship.
The North Korean officer who oversees Hanako's captivity is called _____.
Match each character to their role in the play:
right: Abducted Japanese teenager; the play's central figure across two decades
Hanako's older sister; becomes an adult advocate for the abductees
North Korean assigned to learn Japanese from Hanako; a complex relationship develops

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Hanako in The Great Wave?
flashcard_questions.a: A 17-year-old Japanese girl abducted by North Korean agents; the play's central figure.
Hanako's older sister; the last person to see Hanako; becomes an adult campaigner.
Hanako and Reiko's mother; ages visibly across the play as grief shapes her life.
The North Korean officer overseeing Hanako's captivity; complicit in the regime but humanised.
A North Korean assigned to learn Japanese from Hanako; their relationship evolves across the play.
The deliberate shaping of voice by a performer to reveal a character's inner life.
The physical and psychological distance between performers, communicating relationship and power.
A Brechtian physical posture or gesture expressing a character's social attitude, not personal feeling.
A broad, even coverage of stage area using a Fresnel or flood lantern.
The direction away from the audience, towards the back of the stage.
The direction nearest the audience, at the front of the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What key performance challenge does playing Hanako present?
flashcard_questions.a: Communicating 24 years of interior change through specific vocal and physical evolution.

glossary_terms.definition: The specific choices a performer makes about pitch, pace, volume, pause and intonation to communicate character and emotion.
The physical and psychological distance between performers on stage, used to communicate relationship, power and emotion.
A performance term developed by Brecht for a physical posture or gesture that expresses a character's social attitude rather than personal emotion.
A broad, even coverage of stage area from overhead using a Fresnel or flood lantern, typically used to illuminate a scene generally.
The direction away from the audience, towards the back of the stage.
The direction nearest to the audience, at the front of the stage.
In Stanislavski's method, the factual conditions of a character's life at any given moment in the play, which shape every choice the performer makes.
